stories.headline: OIL SLIDES TO 3-MONTH LOW AS HORMUZ CLOSURE FAILS TO STICK
stories.body: WTI fell about 2.3% to roughly $74, its lowest since early March, even after Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed again on June 20. Lloyd's List data showed tankers still transiting the waterway over the weekend.
stories.explain: Crude prices reflect expected barrels, not headlines. With commercial traffic still moving, a 60-day US-Iran ceasefire holding, and the IEA cutting its 2026 demand-growth forecast by 1.1M bpd, traders unwound the geopolitical risk premium rather than chasing the closure announcement. A 13-month-high dollar made dollar-priced crude costlier abroad, adding downside pressure.

stories.headline: MEGA-CAP TECH DRAGS NASDAQ-100 DOWN AS ALPHABET SINKS 5%
stories.body: The Nasdaq-100 fell about 1.4% while the S&P 500 held to -0.37%. Alphabet dropped 5% on worries over AI-talent departures, with Amazon -4.8% and Microsoft -3%; Super Micro Computer (+15.5%) cushioned the broad index.
stories.explain: The NDX is concentrated in a handful of mega-caps, so AI-leadership wobble hits it harder than the broader S&P 500, where stronger breadth and winners like SMCI offset the damage. The split tape shows the selloff was a rotation out of crowded AI megacaps rather than a market-wide risk-off, leaving the equal-weight picture far calmer than the headline indices.

stories.headline: TWO-YEAR YIELD HITS HIGHEST SINCE FEBRUARY 2025 BEFORE PCE
stories.body: The 2-year Treasury yield rose to about 4.24%, its highest since February 2025, and the 10-year climbed to roughly 4.51% as investors positioned ahead of the Fed's preferred PCE inflation reading later this week.
stories.explain: The 2-year tracks expectations for the Fed's near-term path, so its climb signals markets pricing fewer or later rate cuts. With the curve spread holding near +27 bps, the move is a repricing of policy expectations into firmer inflation data rather than a growth signal, tightening financial conditions even before the central bank acts.

stories.headline: VANCE MEETS IRANIAN DELEGATION IN SWITZERLAND TO SHORE UP TRUCE
stories.body: Vice President JD Vance held high-level talks in Switzerland to clarify terms of the war's end after a 60-day ceasefire signed June 17. Iran's claim it had re-closed Hormuz was disputed by the US military and Lloyd's List shipping data.
stories.explain: Markets treat the conflict as a tail risk on energy supply, so each diplomatic step compresses the embedded oil premium. The gap between Iran's closure rhetoric and observed tanker flows let traders fade the threat, but unresolved final terms keep a floor under volatility in crude, the dollar, and defensive assets like gold.

stories.headline: DOLLAR EXTENDS TO 13-MONTH HIGH AS GOLD STILL GRINDS UP
stories.body: The dollar index pushed to about 101, a fresh 13-month high, on firmer yields and safe-haven demand. Gold rose 0.9% to roughly $4,190 an ounce despite the stronger dollar's usual headwind.
stories.explain: Gold and the dollar normally move inversely, so both rising signals investors hedging geopolitical and inflation risk simultaneously rather than a clean risk-on or risk-off bet. Higher real yields argue against gold, but persistent Middle East uncertainty and central-bank buying are keeping bids under bullion even as the dollar climbs.

stories.headline: TRANSFER PORTAL RESHAPES 2026-27 ROSTERS AS DRAFT WITHDRAWALS LAND
stories.body: Iowa State's Milan Momcilovic (16.9 ppg, 48.7% from three) committed to Kentucky and Wake Forest's Juke Harris (21.4 ppg) chose Tennessee, while 38 players withdrew from the NBA Draft to return to school.

stories.headline: 2026 NBA DRAFT OPENS JUNE 23 WITH WIZARDS HOLDING NO. 1 PICK
stories.body: Washington won the lottery and is on the clock first, with Duke's Cameron Boozer and UNC's Caleb Wilson in the mix. The champion Knicks (beat the Spurs 4-1) and Pistons, at No. 21, round out a deep first round.

stories.headline: SUPER BOWL LX CHAMPION SEAHAWKS WRAP OFFSEASON PROGRAM
stories.body: Seattle received its Super Bowl LX rings on June 11 and closed mandatory minicamp under coach Mike Macdonald's 'run it forward' message. Rookie RB Jadarian Price is competing for early snaps alongside George Holani.

stories.headline: RECRUITING HEATS UP: WESLEY TO TEXAS, O'NEAL FLIPS TO FLORIDA STATE
stories.body: Five-star edge Richard Wesley (No. 11 in the ESPN 300) committed to Texas on June 22, while four-star QB Jaden O'Neal flipped from Oklahoma to Florida State. Florida, Texas and Texas A&M led June's recruiting risers.

deepDive.title: Why Oil Fell on a Strait Closure
content: There was a puzzle on the tape today. On June 20, Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed, the chokepoint through which roughly 20 million barrels of crude move daily, about a fifth of all seaborne oil. A genuine blockade is the textbook trigger for an oil spike. Yet WTI fell about 2.3% to near $74, its lowest since early March. Equity-energy names lagged and gasoline futures eased. For a finance student, the lesson is that prices respond to expected barrels, not to the volume of a headline, and the two diverged sharply.

The key concept is the geopolitical risk premium, the extra dollars buyers pay for the chance of a future supply shock. That premium is an expectation, so it deflates the moment expectations fall. Lloyd's List shipping data showed tankers still transiting Hormuz over the weekend, the US military disputed the closure, and the June 17 ceasefire held for its 60-day window. Layer on the IEA cutting its 2026 demand-growth forecast by 1.1 million barrels per day and a dollar at a 13-month high near 101, and the marginal trade was to sell premium, not buy it.

History rhymes here. The 1980s Tanker War, the 2019 Abqaiq strikes, and the 2024 escalations all produced sharp crude spikes that faded within days or weeks once barrels kept flowing. The recurring pattern: threat lifts price, reality resets it. Global spare capacity, strategic reserves, and the fast supply response of US shale all cap how far a fear-driven rally can run. The market repeatedly distinguishes between a disruption that is announced and one that is actually realized in tanker-tracking and inventory data, and it pays only for the latter.

So the trade today was expectations beating rhetoric, and it is reversible. If tankers genuinely stop and inventories draw, the premium snaps back violently, the kind of convexity that makes energy a portfolio hedge. Absent a real blockage, demand softness and a firm dollar dominate the path of crude. Watch tanker counts, the Fed's PCE print this week, and whether final ceasefire terms hold. The same framework, expected supply versus realized disruption, governs everything from gasoline at the pump to inflation breakevens and the rate path.
